From Projections to Matrix Structure

One Structure, Six Tools

1PSD$A\T A\succeq0$
2SVD$A=U\Sigma V\T$
3PCAspread of data
4Pseudoinverse$x^\star=A^+b$

Why loop back: near a stationary point, a smooth cost changes like the quadratic form of its Hessian.

Definition

Positive Semidefinite Matrices

A Quadratic Form Gives Each Displacement a Height

$$q(x)=x\T Hx=ax_1^2+2bx_1x_2+cx_2^2$$
$x\in\R^2$
the input displacement
$H=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{bmatrix}$
real and symmetric, $H=H\T$
$Hx\in\R^2$
a vector
$q(x)\in\R$
one number: the height, or cost, of $x$

Worked example

$H=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{bmatrix}$, $x=(1,-1)$: $Hx=(1,-2)$, so $x\T(Hx)=1+2=3$. Check: $2-2+3=3$.

Definition

Positive Semidefinite Matrices

Positive Definite and Positive Semidefinite

$$\begin{aligned}H\succ0&\iff x\T Hx>0\ \text{for all } x\neq0\\H\succeq0&\iff x\T Hx\ge0\ \text{for all } x\end{aligned}$$
$H=H\T$
real $n\times n$; both tests assume it
$H\succ0$
positive definite (PD)
$H\succeq0$
positive semidefinite (PSD)

Every PD matrix is PSD. The trough is one PSD matrix that is not PD; the zero matrix is another.

Theorem

Positive Semidefinite Matrices

Eigenvectors Rotate the Form Into Principal Axes

Spectral theorem: real symmetric $H$ has real $\lambda_i$ and orthonormal eigenvectors $v_i$.

$$H=Q\Lambda Q\T,\qquad x\T Hx=z\T\Lambda z=\sum_i\lambda_i z_i^2$$
$Q=[v_1\cdots v_n]$
$Q\T Q=I$: rotation or reflection
$\Lambda$
diagonal $\lambda_i$
$z=Q\T x$
$z_i=v_i\T x$

$H\succeq0\iff$ all $\lambda_i\ge0$
$H\succ0\iff$ all $\lambda_i>0$

Derivation

Positive Semidefinite Matrices

Every Gram Matrix Is PSD

$$x\T A\T Ax=(Ax)\T(Ax)=\|Ax\|^2\ge0$$
$A\in\R^{m\times n}$
any shape: tall, wide or square
$A\T A$
Gram matrix, $n\times n$: $(A\T A)\T=A\T A$
$\ge0$
for every $x\in\R^n$, so $A\T A\succeq0$

Worked example

$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$, $A\T A=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&5\end{bmatrix}$
$x=(1,-1)$: $\|Ax\|^2=\|(-1,-1,1)\|^2=3$
$x\T A\T Ax=2-4+5=3$

Flat Directions Are Null Directions

A₂ =
1  1
0  0
$$\begin{gathered}x\T A\T Ax=\|Ax\|^2=0\iff Ax=0\\ \operatorname{Null}(A\T A)=\operatorname{Null}(A)\end{gathered}$$
$\iff$
a squared length is 0 only for the zero vector
$\operatorname{Null}(A)$
all $x\in\R^n$ with $Ax=0$
why
$A\T Ax=0\Rightarrow x\T A\T Ax=0\Rightarrow Ax=0$; conversely $Ax=0\Rightarrow A\T Ax=0$

Definition

Positive Semidefinite Matrices

The PSD Square Root

$$H^{1/2}=Q\Lambda^{1/2}Q\T,\qquad x\T Hx=\|H^{1/2}x\|^2$$
$H=Q\Lambda Q\T$
PSD: $\lambda_i\ge0$, $Q=[v_1\ v_2]$
$\Lambda^{1/2}$
$\mathrm{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_i})$: real as $\lambda_i\ge0$
$H^{1/2}$
unique symmetric PSD: $H^{1/2}H^{1/2}=H$

Worked example

$H=\mathrm{diag}(4,1)$: $Q=I$, $H^{1/2}=\mathrm{diag}(2,1)$
$x=(1,2)$: $H^{1/2}x=(2,2)$
$\|H^{1/2}x\|^2=8=x\T Hx$

Singular Value Decomposition

The Four Subspaces From U and V

Full SVD: $U$ is $m\times m$, $V$ is $n\times n$. Example: the all-ones $3\times2$ matrix, rank $r=1$.

$\mathrm{Row}(A)=\mathrm{span}(v_1,\dots,v_r)$, dim $r$

$\mathrm{Null}(A)=\mathrm{span}(v_{r+1},\dots,v_n)$, dim $n-r$

$\mathrm{Col}(A)=\mathrm{span}(u_1,\dots,u_r)$, dim $r$

$\mathrm{Null}(A\T)=\mathrm{span}(u_{r+1},\dots,u_m)$, dim $m-r$

Theorem

Singular Value Decomposition

The Best Rank-k Approximation

$$A_k=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_iu_iv_i\T\in\arg\min_{\operatorname{rank}B\le k}\|A-B\|_F$$
$\|M\|_F^2$
$\sum_{i,j}M_{ij}^2$
$\|A-A_k\|_F^2$
$\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$, the error
$k$
$0\le k\le r$; $A_r=A$
$B$
any matrix with $\operatorname{rank}\le k$
Eckart–Young
no proof; may not be unique if $\sigma_k=\sigma_{k+1}>0$

Definition

Principal Component Analysis

Data as a Matrix: One Row per Sample

$$X=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\T\\ \vdots\\ x_N\T\end{bmatrix}\in\R^{N\times d}$$
$x_j\in\R^d$
sample $j$: one point in feature space
$N$
rows = samples; here $N=8$
$d$
columns = features; here $d=2$

Sixteen numbers, but a thin cloud. Could one number per sample nearly do?

Which Line Best Summarizes the Cloud?

  1. Athe horizontal line

  3. Cthe short-axis line

Definition

Principal Component Analysis

Centering Moves the Mean to the Origin

$$\mu=\frac1N\sum_{j=1}^{N}x_j,\qquad X_c=X-\mathbf 1\mu\T$$
$\mu\in\R^d$
mean sample, in feature space
$\mathbf 1\in\R^N$
all ones; $\mathbf 1\mu\T$ is $N\times d$, each row $\mu\T$
$X_c$
$N\times d$, row $j$ is $(x_j-\mu)\T$; columns sum to $0$

Worked example

Row sums $(24,16)$: $\mu=(3,2)$; $x_1\approx(-0.18,0.51)$, $x_1-\mu\approx(-3.18,-1.49)$

Principal Component Analysis

What Does an Uncentered SVD Find?

Definition

Principal Component Analysis

Sample Covariance and Directional Variance

$$C=\frac{X_c\T X_c}{N-1},\qquad \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j}(x_{c,j}\T v)^2=v\T Cv$$
$x_{c,j}\T$
row $j$ of $X_c$
$v\in\R^d$
unit direction
left side
variance of the $N$ projections (mean $0$): sum of squares over $N-1$
$C$
$d\times d$, symmetric, PSD; $N>1$

Worked example

$v=e_1$: $v\T Cv=C_{11}=31.68/7\approx4.53$, the variance of feature 1.

$$\text{kept}_k=\frac{\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_i^2}{\sum_i\sigma_i^2}$$

The Pseudoinverse

$$A^+=V_r\Sigma_r^{-1}U_r\T=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\frac{1}{\sigma_i}v_iu_i\T$$

Definition

Pseudoinverse and Conditioning

Minimum-Norm Least Squares

First minimize the residual $\|b-Ax\|$; then take the smallest norm among tied minimizers.

$$x=x^\star+z:\quad\|x\|^2=\|x^\star\|^2+\|z\|^2$$
$x$
any minimizer; $z\in{}$Null($A$)
$x^\star=A^+b$
in Row($A$), so $x^\star\perp z$
$\|x\|^2$
squared norm: least only at $z=0$

Worked example

Along $u_2$: $0.1/0.25=0.4$ mm along $v_2$: 8 times.

1    0
0 0.01

Both output errors have length $0.01$. Which gives the larger input error $\|\delta x\|$?

  1. A$\delta b=(0.01,\,0)$

Definition

Pseudoinverse and Conditioning

Condition Number and Numerical Rank

$$\|A\|_2=\sigma_{\max},\quad\kappa_2(A)=\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}},\quad r_\tau=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}$$
$\|A\|_2,r_\tau$
any $A$, $\tau\ge0$
$\kappa_2$
full rank; else $\infty$ by convention
$1/\sigma_{\min}$
absolute; $\kappa_2$ relative, worst case
scope
exact $Ax=b$, only $b$ moves

Conditioning is the problem’s, stability the algorithm’s.

Pseudoinverse and Conditioning

Which Matrix Is Worse Conditioned?

Image ellipses of $A$ and $B$ at one scale. Which is worse conditioned?

  1. A$A=\mathrm{diag}(10,1)$
  2. B$B=\mathrm{diag}(2,1)$
  3. Cequally conditioned

Definition

Pseudoinverse and Conditioning

Damped Least Squares

$$x_\lambda=\arg\min_x(\|Ax-b\|^2+\lambda^2\|x\|^2)=\sum_{\sigma_i>0}\frac{\sigma_i\,u_i\T b}{\sigma_i^2+\lambda^2}v_i$$
$\lambda>0$
damping, a number we choose
$x_\lambda$
solves $(A\T A+\lambda^2 I)x=A\T b$: always unique
$\sigma_i/(\sigma_i^2+\lambda^2)$
damped gain; $0$ when $\sigma_i=0$

Bounded amplification: every damped gain is at most $1/(2\lambda)$.

Fix $A,b$. As $\lambda$ grows $0\to3$, what do $\|x_\lambda\|$ and $\|r_\lambda\|$ do?

  2. B$\|x_\lambda\|$ increases, $\|r_\lambda\|$ always decreases
  3. C$b$ stays exactly attained

Choosing a Solver

SolverNeedsGives
thin QR, Lecture 3full column rank$R\hat x=Q\T b$
SVDany $A$$A^+b$, minimum norm
damped$\lambda>0$$x_\lambda$ (new objective), gains $\le1/(2\lambda)$
$$\kappa_2(A\T A)=\kappa_2(A)^2$$
$A$, $r=n$
$\kappa_2=\sigma_1/\sigma_n$
$A\T A$
gains $\sigma_i^2$

In code, solve systems, never invert. QR exists for every $A$.

Forward Kinematics Is Nonlinear

$$p=f(q),\qquad q\in\R^n,\ \ p\in\R^m$$
$q$
joint vector: $n$ angles in radians here; a prismatic joint would contribute a length
$p$
tip position only: $m$ task coordinates, no orientation
$f$
forward kinematics: sines and cosines of $q$, not a matrix

Recall

Jacobians and Robot Motion

The Derivative as a Local Gain

$$f(q+\Delta q)\approx f(q)+f'(q)\,\Delta q$$
$f'(q)$
local gain: output change per radian, at this $q$
$\Delta q$
step in radians; for small steps the model error shrinks like $\Delta q^2$

Worked example

$q=30^\circ$: $f=0.5$, $f'=\cos30^\circ\approx0.866$. Step $\Delta q=0.2$ rad: model $\approx0.673$, actual $\approx0.662$.

Definition

Jacobians and Robot Motion

The Jacobian Matrix

$$J_{ij}(q)=\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial q_j}(q),\qquad J(q)\in\R^{m\times n}$$
row $i$
output $p_i=f_i(q)$, $i=1,\dots,m$
column $j$
joint $q_j$, $j=1,\dots,n$; the other joints held fixed
$$\Delta p\approx J(q)\,\Delta q$$
$\Delta q\in\R^n$
a small joint change, in radians; $\Delta p\in\R^m$

  3. C$7\times7$

Jacobians and Robot Motion

Columns Are Joint Effects

$$J=\begin{bmatrix}j_1&\cdots&j_n\end{bmatrix},\ \ J\Delta q=\sum_{j=1}^{n}j_j\,\Delta q_j$$
$j_j\in\R^m$
column $j$: tip length per radian of joint $j$ alone
$\Delta q_j$
how far joint $j$ turns; the contributions add
$j_j(q)$
changes with the pose $q$

Drawn: $\dot p=J\dot q$ at $\dot q=(1,1)$ rad/s, $q=(30^\circ,60^\circ)$: velocities, not paths.

$\partial p/\partial q_1$
$$j_2=\begin{bmatrix}-l_2\sin q_{12}\\l_2\cos q_{12}\end{bmatrix}$$

$\partial p/\partial q_2$

$$J=U\Sigma V\T,\qquad Jv_i=\sigma_i u_i$$

unit tip direction in task space

J(30°,90°) ≈
−1.37 −0.87
 0.37 −0.50
$$\dot q^\star=J^+\dot p_{\rm d}$$
$\dot p_{\rm d}$
desired tip velocity

Redundancy and Null Motion

$$\dot q=J^+\dot p_{\rm d}+z,\qquad Jz=0$$
$J$
$2\times3$: two tip coordinates, three joints, rank 2

Each finite step: first order only

Damping and Relinearization

$$\dot q_\lambda=J\T(JJ\T+\lambda^2I)^{-1}\dot p_{\rm d},\quad\lambda>0$$
$J$
$m\times n$ at this $q$
$JJ\T+\lambda^2I$
$m\times m$, positive definite
stepslargest model errorfinal target error

Definition

Hessians and Local Curvature

From Vector Outputs to a Scalar Objective

$$f:\R^n\to\R,\qquad \nabla f(x)\in\R^{n},\qquad H(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)\in\R^{n\times n}$$
$f(x)$
one number, the objective at parameters $x$
$\nabla f(x)$
$n\times1$, the local slope, pointing uphill
$H(x)$
$n\times n$, how $\nabla f$ changes as $x$ moves; same letter as the quadratic forms, on purpose
$J(q)$
vector output $p(q)\in\R^m$: $m\times n$

Vote

Hessians and Local Curvature

Which Curve Has a Local Minimum at 0?

All three have $f'(0)=0$. Which one has a local minimum at $t=0$?

  1. A$f(t)=t^2$
  2. B$f(t)=-t^2$
  3. C$f(t)=t^3$

Definition

Hessians and Local Curvature

The Hessian Matrix

$$H_{ij}(x)=\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_i\,\partial x_j}(x),\qquad i,j=1,\dots,n$$
$H_{ij}$
how the slope $\partial f/\partial x_j$ changes when $x_i$ moves
$f\in C^2$
second partials continuous near $x$
then
$H_{ij}=H_{ji}$: $H=H\T$, symmetric $n\times n$

Model

Hessians and Local Curvature

The Second-Order Approximation

$$f(x+\Delta x)\approx f(x)+\nabla f(x)\T\Delta x+\frac12\Delta x\T H(x)\Delta x$$
$x$
fixed expansion point; $f\in C^2$
$\Delta x$
small step
$\nabla f$
$n\times1$, tilt: tangent plane
$H$
$n\times n$, bend: quadratic model

Worked example

$f=e^{x_1}-1-x_1+\frac12(x_2-x_1)^2$, $x=(0,1)$: $f(x)=\frac12$, $\nabla f=(-1,1)$, $H=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$

  1. A200$\frac12$
  2. B4001
  3. C1004

Definition

Hessians and Local Curvature

Curvature Along a Direction

$$g(t)=f(x+tv),\qquad g''(0)=v\T H(x)\,v$$
$v$
direction, unit: $\|v\|=1$, so directions compare fairly
$g$
height of $f$ along the line through $x$
$g''(0)$
second derivative along that line, not the surface's geometric curvature
why
$g'(t)=\nabla f(x+tv)\T v$; differentiate once more
here
$f=\tfrac12x\T Hx$, $H=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$, $x=0$

Second-derivative test

Hessians and Local Curvature

Classifying a Stationary Point

$$f(x^\star+\Delta x)\approx f(x^\star)+\tfrac12\Delta x\T H(x^\star)\Delta x$$

Local tests only. $f\in C^2$ on a convex open set: convex $\iff H(x)\succeq0$ at every $x$.

$x^\star,\Delta x$
stationary point ($\nabla f=0$), small step
$f$
$C^2$ near $x^\star$: $H$ symmetric $n\times n$
$\lambda_i$
eigenvalues of $H(x^\star)$: their signs decide

at $(0,0)$
